children: By Neil Mehta, Yoko Kubota and Lindsay Wise

WASHINGTON-With just weeks to go before midterm elections, Senate Republicans defeated a resolution to curb President Trump's ability to wage war against Iran, even as a growing number of GOP incumbents and candidates in tough races insist they want the war to end soon.

The measure was defeated in a 50-49 vote, largely along party lines. One Democrat, Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman, voted with most Republicans to oppose the resolution, which would have directed the president to remove U.S. troops from hostilities against Iran. Four Republicans-Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska-voted with all other Democrats in favor of the measure.

Democrats pointed to the Iran conflict for driving costs higher. "Our Wisconsin farmers are just getting hammered," said Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D., Wis.). "Small-business owners are trying to stay afloat."

For Republicans, the vote marked a high-profile opportunity to signal disagreement with President Trump over his handling of the Iran war before heading home to campaign. Spiking gas and diesel prices have become a major vulnerability for the GOP, and polls consistently rank the cost of living as a top issue for voters.

Tillis, who had voted against previous Iran measures, said he might have voted no again if he had been properly briefed and convinced that the war was on the right track. He said he came close Wednesday, when senators got what he described as "a good brief" from U.S. Central Command's commander Adm. Brad Cooper. But he said it was "not enough and too late."

Voter anger over gas prices has already bled into midterm elections, as Senate Republicans try to hang on to their 53-47 majority. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R., S.D.) called war-powers measures "political votes" but said that Republicans running in the midterms should be able to break with Trump, painting it as a pragmatic move that could help some candidates win votes.
"I think they need to be their own person," he said. "And I think that's the best way to win."

In the U.S., diesel prices have vaulted to new records in the wake of the missile strikes that have crippled fuel-making facilities in the Middle East and Russia. The national average for a gallon of diesel reached $6.51 Thursday, up nearly a dollar over the past month, according to AAA.
Sen. Joni Ernst (R., Iowa) said farmers heading into harvest season want to be assured that diesel prices would come down.

"I would like the administration to come back with a very clear plan on how they bring this to an end," Ernst, who is set to retire after this term, said Wednesday. "I do support the president, but this is really having an impact on everyday Americans."

Democrats have seized on the war as a potent campaign issue, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.) criticizing Trump on the floor this week. "Trump needs to reckon with the cost of his catastrophic blunder in Iran," he said.

This week, several Republicans facing tight races sought quick action to address energy prices. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R., Iowa), who is running for the open Senate seat in the state, called on the Trump administration to pause diesel exports, arguing Iowans "shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran."

Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, who is running for Senate in Michigan, also called for a pause in diesel exports and said the "war in Iran needs to end to bring costs down." Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin, said Tuesday, "I just believe we should be exiting Iran, that it's time to move on."

The resolution, which previously passed the House 214-208, is largely symbolic and won't go to the president's desk for his signature or a veto. Legal scholars largely view such "concurrent resolutions" as nonbinding because of a Supreme Court decision in the 1980s that found similar measures to be unconstitutional legislative vetoes.
Thursday marked the 14th time that the Senate has voted on an Iran war-powers resolution since the war started.

In June, four Senate Republicans joined with Democrats, 50-48, to narrowly approve a concurrent resolution to limit Trump's ability to conduct military operations against Iran without congressional authorization. The House already had passed the same resolution on June 3, in a 215-208 vote, with four Republicans joining Democrats in support.
